opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, Xiaojun, it's great to be here.

When we started Galbot, we had to make a very honest assessment of where the real bottleneck in embodied intelligence is. I believe the bottleneck today is not the hardware itself. It's the brain: the ability of a robot to generalize, to perceive an unfamiliar environment, to grasp an object it has never seen before, and to do that reliably enough that someone will actually pay for it.

If you look at the hardware side, many components are already quite mature. Industrial arms, mobile bases, motors, reducers, cameras, and depth sensors have been refined over decades of automation and consumer electronics. They are reliable, the supply chains are established, and the costs keep coming down. If we as a startup tried to reinvent every joint and actuator from scratch, we would spend years and enormous amounts of capital on problems that aren't what's holding the field back. Meanwhile the intelligence problem would still be unsolved.

So our philosophy is to put our effort where the marginal value is highest. We build the robot body from proven, stable parts so it behaves predictably, and we focus our research on the models, the data, and the learning pipeline.

That connects to our emphasis on synthetic data and simulation. To train a generalizable model, you need huge amounts of data, and real-world teleoperation alone is too slow and too expensive. We generate massive amounts of data in simulation, for example large-scale grasping data with physically realistic rendering, and then transfer it to the real robot. For that sim-to-real transfer to work, the real hardware has to be well characterized and consistent. If your hardware is exotic or keeps changing, your simulation never matches reality, and the whole data flywheel breaks down. Mature hardware gives us a stable target to model, which is what makes large-scale simulated training practical.

Then there's commercialization. A robot deployed in a pharmacy, a retail store, or a factory has to work every day. Customers don't care how novel your actuator design is. They care about uptime, safety, and cost. Proven components let us move toward real deployments sooner, and those deployments generate real-world data that feeds back into our models. That loop between deployment and data matters more to us than having the flashiest hardware.

Just as important is what we choose not to do yet. We use wheels instead of legs for many scenarios. Legs are impressive in demos, but for most indoor commercial settings with flat floors, wheels are more stable, more efficient, and cheaper. Our view is: don't add complexity unless the task truly requires it.

This doesn't mean hardware innovation is unimportant. Over time, as the models get stronger, we'll understand much better what the body really needs, such as better hands, better tactile sensing, and better force control, and we'll push hardware forward in those targeted directions. But I think the right sequence is to let the intelligence lead, and let the hardware evolve in service of what the brain can actually use.

r001.rationale: It says reinventing joints and actuators from scratch would consume years and capital on hardware problems while the intelligence problem remains unsolved, and that exotic or changing hardware complicates development and sim-to-real transfer. This communicates the burden of tackling hardware production issues alongside embodied intelligence development.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Because I think the hard part right now isn't the hardware. The hard part is the brain.

When we started Galbot, we looked at the robotics landscape and asked ourselves: where is the actual bottleneck? For decades, people were building very sophisticated mechanical systems, humanoids with dozens of degrees of freedom, custom actuators, exotic sensors. And those robots still couldn't reliably pick up a cup. The limitation wasn't that the arm couldn't reach the cup. It was that the robot didn't understand the cup, didn't perceive the scene well, couldn't generalize to a cup it had never seen before. That's a software problem, a learning problem.

So my view is, if you're building a company around embodied AI, you should spend your scarce resources on the thing that is actually unsolved. Mature components, standard arms, commercial grippers, off-the-shelf depth cameras, these already work. They've been debugged by thousands of engineers over many years. They're reliable, they're affordable, and critically, they're available at scale. If I design a novel hand with tactile skin, I might spend two years and a lot of money just getting it to not break, and during those two years I've collected zero data and trained zero models.

There's a second reason that's related to data. A learning-based approach lives and dies on how much interaction data you can gather. If your hardware is proven and cheap, you can deploy ten, fifty, a hundred robots quickly and start collecting. If it's bespoke and fragile, you have three prototypes and they're always in the repair shop. The data flywheel never starts turning.

And a third point: proven hardware makes the research cleaner. When something fails, I want to know it failed because the policy was wrong, not because a motor overheated or a custom sensor drifted. Removing hardware uncertainty lets the team iterate on algorithms much faster.

Now, I'm not saying hardware doesn't matter or that we'll never build our own. As the models get better, they start to expose limitations in the body, and then you redesign the body around what the brain actually needs. But that sequencing matters. Let the intelligence tell you what hardware to build, rather than guessing up front. That's the philosophy.

r001.rationale: The response says bespoke hardware can be fragile, costly to get working, and difficult to scale, but does not clearly state that components unproven in mass production make development contend with hardware production problems at the same time.

astra-6.text:
Because our goal at Galbot is to develop embodied intelligence, we want a reliable hardware foundation on which to build and test it. If the hardware and the intelligence are both changing at the same time, it becomes difficult to tell why a task failed. Was it the model, the controller, or a mechanical problem?

Using proven components reduces that uncertainty and lets us focus more of our effort on perception, decision-making, and manipulation. It also makes data collection more consistent: we can run more experiments and learn from the results instead of spending so much time troubleshooting the platform.

That doesn’t mean hardware innovation is unimportant. Hardware and intelligence ultimately have to work together. But we prefer to start with something dependable, identify the limitations through real tasks, and then make hardware changes where there is a clear need.

r001.rationale: The candidate says changing hardware and intelligence together makes failures harder to diagnose and increases platform troubleshooting. It does not explain that components unproven in mass production create hardware production problems during development.

sol-6.1.text:
At Galbot, our main goal is to develop embodied intelligence, so we want a reliable hardware foundation. If we develop every component ourselves, we’re tackling mechanical reliability and intelligence at the same time. When something goes wrong, it becomes difficult to tell whether the problem comes from the hardware or the algorithm.

Using proven components lets us focus on perception, decision-making, and control, and iterate more quickly. It also gives us a consistent platform for collecting data and testing what the robot has learned. That doesn’t mean the hardware can never change. We can improve it as we discover specific limitations, but we want those decisions to come from what the intelligence actually needs.

r001.rationale: The response says that developing components in-house would require addressing mechanical reliability alongside intelligence development. It does not mention whether those components are proven in mass production or identify mass-production problems.
